input.new_string:
Build and test commands are in `AGENTS.md`.

### B10. Match the mockup in the real app

Green tests do not prove the panel looks right. A previous slice of this UI
had 267 passing harness checks and two rendering defects that only opening
the image revealed. Part B is not done until the real Agent panel has been
compared against the mockup, row by row, and every discrepancy is either
fixed or written down with a reason.

**The reference.** `print-timeline-panel-full · no revert`, node `553-86`, on
the Main Page of the JusPrin v2 Figma file, 429 px wide. Export it from Figma
as PNG at 1x and 2x. The Figma MCP server is on a plan with a monthly call
cap, so export through the Figma editor in a browser rather than through the
MCP tools, or ask Kenneth for the export.

**The real thing.** Drive the built app, not a React preview, to the state
the mockup shows: a conversation with a user message, an Agent reply with a
collapsed settings diff, "Answered · nothing changed" under a reply, a run of
manual edits shown as merged rows with the "you, on the plate · N steps
merged · time" metadata line, a G-code entry, and a print outcome. Seed that
from a fixture `state.json` plus real edits in the harness rather than by
hand. Capture the panel from inside the app: the shell harness already has a
capture scenario (`--recomputing-capture <dir>`, `tests/shell/shell_harness.cpp:50`,
`begin_recomputing_capture` at `:1288`) and writes bitmaps for fork-owned
controls (`capture_chip_appearance`, `:884`); add a `--timeline-capture <dir>`
scenario in the same style. Capture at 100% and 200% display scaling, light
and dark, on macOS, and at least once on the Windows VM
(`/Users/kenneth/jusprin-win-vm-harness/`, see its README), since text there
renders about 9% larger.

**The comparison.** Put the export and the capture side by side at the same
pixel scale and go through the mockup top to bottom. Check, for each row
kind: vertical rhythm and gaps, hairline positions and color, left inset and
icon, type role and weight of the title and the metadata line, text color
tokens, the merged-steps wording, the "Answered · nothing changed" marker,
ordering among G-code entries and print outcomes, and how a long label
truncates or wraps. Every value must come from the token file through the
design-system rules; a value that exists in the mockup but not in the tokens
gets a token first, never a literal (`agent-docs/jusprin/design-system.md`,
"Writing UI code").

**What counts as a good reason not to match.** Only these: glyph
rasterization and sub-pixel differences between Figma and the platform text
engine; a platform font metric that shifts a baseline by a pixel; a WebView
or wxWidgets limitation that cannot be worked around without an OrcaSlicer
change. Not acceptable: a different size, weight, color, spacing, inset,
missing hairline, missing element, different wording, or different order.
"Close enough" is not a reason.

**Deliverable.** In the PR description, a table with one line per
discrepancy found: what differed, the fix, or the reason it was left, with
the before and after captures attached. If the table is empty, say what was
compared and attach the captures anyway.

content.text:
The Figma copy is verified and both documents are updated. Nothing is left running.

**Figma check.** The new frame `print-timeline-panel-full · no revert` sits beside the original on the Main Page. At 100% the agent's settings card flows straight into the "Rotated bracket to 45°" and "Infill 35% → 45%" rows with normal spacing, the G-code entries and print outcome are unchanged, and the frame shrank from 1599 to 1500 px, which matches the removed card. The original frame still has its revert card.

**[revision-timeline-handoff.md](agent-docs/jusprin/revision-timeline-handoff.md)** is rewritten around the decision, in two parts to be landed as separate commits:

- **Part A, remove Revert.** A "Keep" list first, because over-deletion is the likely mistake: the clean-sharing export, the workspace change counter also called `revision` and everything staleness-related built on it, the manufacturing records minus their revision field, and two comments about OrcaSlicer's own preset revert. Then a file-by-file inventory with line numbers of what goes: persistence capture and restore, the document's revision records and truncation, the two bridge messages, the page component, store and protocol entries, styles, the C++ and Vitest cases, the shell harness Phase 4 and Phase 6 revert scenarios, and the state file compatibility rule. A "done when" section gives a grep that must come back clean and requires no OrcaSlicer file to change.
- **Part B, build the change log.** The undo-history rule, raw recording, the state file array, the row grouping per the no-revert mockup, simplest labels with the empty-name fallback, the one-line dirty hook, the two accepted holes, the adapter and persistence guide, and the test list.
- **B10, match the mockup.** Per your message: the agent must drive the real built app to the mockup's state, capture the panel from inside the app using the shell harness's existing capture pattern at 100% and 200% scaling in light and dark and once on the Windows VM, compare row by row against a Figma export, and fix every discrepancy. The only accepted reasons not to match are glyph rasterization, a one-pixel platform baseline shift, or a WebView or wxWidgets limitation that would need an OrcaSlicer change. The PR must carry a discrepancy table with before and after captures.

**One thing to know.** The bridge spec document this work used to cite was untracked in an earlier commit titled "Stop tracking transient Agent handoff", so all references to it are gone from both documents. The spike document's banner now says Revert was dropped entirely and records the two restore-point designs considered, in case the feature ever returns.

Your Figma prompt listed "coalesced manual-edit entries" among the things to keep, so I kept the work that produces them.

2. **Drop the rows too.** Part B is deleted from the handoff, the Figma copy loses the manual-edit rows and the "nothing changed" marker, and the timeline is chat plus G-code entries plus print outcomes. Part A alone then finishes the timeline.

Tell me which, and I'll cut the handoff to match.

**Your instruction about examining the real UI.** It is in the handoff as section B10, "Match the mockup in the real app": drive the built app to the mockup's state, capture the panel from inside the app at 100% and 200% scaling in light and dark and once on the Windows VM, compare row by row against a Figma export, fix every discrepancy, and only accept glyph rasterization, a one-pixel platform baseline shift, or a WebView or wxWidgets limitation as reasons not to match, with a discrepancy table and before-and-after captures in the PR. The handoff now says it plainly, in three places the coding agent cannot miss.

**At the top, a scope rule in your words:** everything that exists to implement "Revert here" is removed, and what gets built is no more than the change log needed to draw the rows the mockup shows. No restore points, no project state saved by JusPrin, no hooks left "for later". If a piece of code is not needed to draw a row in the mockup, do not write it.

**Part B is retitled "build just enough change log to draw the mockup's rows"** and opens by naming exactly the three things the mockup needs that are not chat: the merged manual-edit row with its metadata line, the settings-change row with the preset name, and "Answered · nothing changed". The stored entry is limited to kind, raw name, actor, time, and the conversation item it follows. An explicit out-of-scope list follows: no marker, no settings record, no file besides the entry array in the state file, no new bridge messages beyond pushing entries, no changes to build or print records, and not the G-code redesign.

**Two small clarifications so "just enough" is not read two ways.** Undo and redo are recorded because a row saying "Rotated" would otherwise stay on screen after the person undid it; it is the same detection code, not a feature. And the settings row reuses the existing delta code the settings card already uses, so it can read "Infill 35% → 45%" without new diff code, while edit rows keep the plain undo-step name. B5 also states that B10's pixel comparison is about layout, type, color and spacing, not the words in an edit row, so the two instructions do not conflict.

The only remaining uses of "restore point" or "marker" in the document are in the scope rule, the out-of-scope list, the history section, and the names of the React component and CSS classes that Part A deletes.

## Writing UI code

Rules for anyone, human or agent, adding or changing a JusPrin surface. They
exist because every value that is typed by hand drifts from Figma and from
the other side of the app within weeks; today's guards catch most of it, but
only if the code goes through the token file in the first place.

1. **Never type a color, radius, font, or control size.** Every one comes
   from `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json`. Native code reads it
   through `ShellTheme`: `palette(dark)` for color, `metrics()` for radii,
   spacing, and per-component sizes, `font(role)` for type. A stock
   `wxStaticText`, `wxTextCtrl`, or OrcaSlicer `Button` is
   dressed through `Shell/ShellRecipes.hpp`, never by calling its setters
   with literals. The Agent page uses only `var(--…)`: `--<group>-<name>` for
   color, `--radius-<name>`, `--font-<role>`, `--font-code`, and
   `--button-<recipe>-padding`.
2. **If the value you need has no token, add the token first.** Put it in
   the JSON, extend the guard in `tests/brand/test_brand_tokens.cpp` so a
   later edit cannot silently move it, then read it from code. Do not write
   the number "for now": the guards cannot see a literal that is already
   there, and the next reader cannot tell a decision from an accident. A
   value that exists in Figma but not in the roles or scales is a design
   decision to raise, not a reason to type it.
3. **Layout spacing may stay literal, on the scale.** Padding between
   regions, gaps, and margins use 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, or 48 DIP.
   Control padding is not layout spacing; it comes from a button recipe.
4. **Pick the nearest role, never a bespoke size.** The roles are the whole
   type system. Bold at a body or label size is a role of its own; if a
   surface seems to need a size that no role has, see rule 2.
5. **Read the code on `jusprin-newui`, not old commit messages or Figma,
   when they disagree.** The header's chip and menu dimensions were once
   changed to match Figma and reverted because they looked worse; the
   token file records what stayed.
6. **Run the guards before calling UI work done:** `brand_tokens_tests`,
   `shell_theme_tests`, and `npm test` in `AgentUI`. Then look at the surface
   in the running app; the guards prove the code went through the tokens,
   not that the result looks right.
7. **Upstream files are off limits for style.** OrcaSlicer's own screens are
   retinted through the hooks `BrandPalette.cpp` installs and nothing else;
   see [Fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md). Their radii and fonts stay
   OrcaSlicer's until the surface is replaced.

**What the 2 px is.** I checked the mockup in Figma. The manual-edit row's text column is a vertical auto-layout with a 2 px gap between the 13/18 title and the 12/16 metadata line, 36 px tall. The G-code destination row's text column is built the same way, also 2 px. So this is the thread's row pattern, not a stray value. Figma's own Spacing variable collection does not contain 2 either; the component types it in. The "Answered · nothing changed" marker sits 4 px under its reply, which is on the scale.

**Why the guard is right to reject it.** The design-system rule is that layout spacing stays on the scale of 4 to 48, and any value that exists in Figma but not in the scales is a design decision to raise, not a number to type. The Vitest guard enforces that on every padding, margin and gap line. Adding 2 to the scale would change the documented scale in four places and invite 2 px layout gaps everywhere.

**What to do instead, now in the handoff.** Treat it as a component metric, which the token file already has a home for alongside the menu row inset and the popover row gap:

1. Add a `threadRow.lineGap` of 2 under the component section of the token file.
2. Pin it in the C++ token guard the way the agent pane sizes are pinned.
3. Emit it from the page's token loader as a CSS variable next to the button padding variables, and register the name so the stylesheet guard's "every requested variable is emitted" check covers it.
4. Use that variable as the row column's gap. The guard only inspects pixel literals, so this passes for the right reason.

The handoff also forbids the two ways to cheat, a padding or line-height trick or a non-pixel unit, and notes that the existing history card column uses 4 where the mockup uses 2, which the G-code entry task should fix with the same variable. The updated file is on the Windows VM.

**Something you should know.** Both handoff documents were missing from the working tree when I went to edit, for the second time in two days, with git status clean. I recovered them from the Entire checkpoint branch, which had my latest versions, and they are back. I could not tell what removes them; they are untracked, so a `git clean` or a stash from any tool would take them. If you want them to stop disappearing, `git add` them.

content.text:
You're right to push back. I said "between rows", and that was wrong. Let me restate it plainly.

**Where the 2 px is.** Inside one row, between that row's two lines of text: the title line and the smaller metadata line under it. Rows themselves are 8 px apart, which is on the scale.

**Is 2 on the spacing scale?** No. The spacing scale is for space between things in a layout: between rows, around regions, margins. It goes 4, 8, 12 and up. A 2 px gap between two lines inside a single row is not layout spacing, so it does not belong on that scale, and adding it there would let people use 2 px between anything.

**Why I call it a component size.** The token file already has a category for numbers that describe how one control is built inside, separate from layout spacing: button padding, the menu row's inset, the popover's row gap. The 2 px between a row's title and its metadata line is the same kind of number. Put it there, and the guards accept it because it is declared, not typed inline.

**Does Figma need to change?** No. Figma types the 2 px directly into the component, which is fine for an internal size. Nothing to adjust unless you decide you would rather have 4 px there, which would make each row 2 px taller.

content.text:
It is true, but not where you might expect. The two spacing scales are identical. The drift is in the Figma frames, which do not use Figma's own scale.

**The scales agree.** Figma's Spacing collection holds exactly 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48. The code's token file holds the same nine values, guarded by a C++ test and a stylesheet test. The code's scale came first, on 2026-08-26, in the commit that documented the design system; the Figma variables were created to match on 2026-09-08.

**The frames ignore the scale.** I measured the auto-layout gaps and paddings in the timeline mockup. Nothing is bound to a variable; every value is typed in. Most are on the scale, but the thread structure drawn this week is not:

| Figma element | Figma value | On scale | App today |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gap between thread items | 14 | no | 8 |
| Gap inside an agent turn | 7 | no | 8 |
| Gap inside a G-code entry | 5 | no | 4 |
| Bottom padding of a G-code entry | 10 | no | 8 |
| Gap between a row's title and metadata | 2 | no | 4 |
| Thread side padding | 16 | yes | 12 |
| Pinned setup, composer, print card padding | 12 | yes | 12 |

**Why they drifted.** Three causes, in order of weight.

1. **Figma has no guard.** The code rejects any off-scale number at test time. Figma accepts anything typed into a field, and a variable only helps if someone binds it. The radius variables show the same thing: the component radii are typed, not bound, and the variables themselves have been edited since 2026-09-08 without the components following.
2. **The new frames were drawn by eye.** The timeline mockup was produced on 2026-09-10 with values like 14, 7, 5 and 2 chosen for visual rhythm. Nobody drawing them was working from the scale, and nothing told them they had left it.
3. **The rule says code wins, so nobody reconciles Figma.** The design-system rule is to read the code when Figma disagrees, because past attempts to match Figma were reverted for looking worse. That rule keeps the code clean, but it also means Figma is never corrected, so each new frame starts from whatever the last one had.

**What follows.** The coding agent's question about the 14 px item gap is one instance of this, not a token decision on its own. The choice is between fixing the frames to the scale, which means changing 14, 7, 5 and 10 to neighbors on the scale and accepting a slightly different rhythm, or accepting that the thread has its own internal sizes and recording them as component tokens the way the 2 px line gap was. Either is defensible. Mixing them per value, which is what is happening now, is what produces the drift.

"Both sides" means the Figma file and the code's token file. Each has the same nine spacing steps.

**My suggestion: fix Figma, keep the scale, and make one exception.**

Most of the off-scale numbers in the timeline mockup, 14, 7, 5 and 10, have no design reason. They are what you get drawing by eye, and each sits one or two pixels from a scale step. The scale exists to remove exactly that noise. Snap them in Figma: 7 to 8, 5 to 4, 10 to 8 or 12, and 14 to 12 or 16, your pick. Nobody will see the difference, and the code needs no new tokens.

The 2 px gap between a row's title and its metadata line is different. It has a structural reason, two text sizes stacked inside one row, and it recurs in every row kind. Keep it, as the component token already in the handoff.

Then stop the drift at its source: in Figma, bind every gap and padding to the Spacing variables instead of typing numbers. A bound value shows as a pill; a typed number is then the tell. Before a frame is handed to a coding agent, have the Figma agent list every gap and padding that is not a variable. That check takes a minute and would have caught all five of these.

```text
Design the JusPrin home screen from the attached wireframe ("5b Work-first · projects gallery, printer cabinet"). Pixel-perfect, using this file's design system. Add it to the Main Page as two frames, home-light and home-dark, 1280×800, placed to the right of prepare-first-print-light.

What the wireframe means. The home screen is a project gallery with a slim printer cabinet on the right. Projects are the main content: a grid of cards, each with a thumbnail, the project name, and a one-line status. The cabinet lists the user's printers: the active one expanded with its live state, connection, nozzle, loaded filaments, and an action to open its monitor; other printers collapsed to a name and a status dot; an "Add printer" affordance at the bottom.

Ignore these parts of the wireframe. They are wireframe habits, not design:
1. The "ORCA" wordmark. Wrong product. Use the JusPrin header chrome from prepare-first-print-light (wordmark, settings) so this screen matches the rest of the app.
2. The "Home" label beside the logo. A home screen has nowhere to go "home" to. Drop it.
3. The italic handwritten face on "New", "Launch monitor" and the caption. Everything is HarmonyOS Sans via the file's text styles.
4. Dashed borders on "Import" and "+ Add printer". Dashed reads as a drop zone. Use Button/Secondary for Import and the file's existing add-item pattern for Add printer.
5. Red as the status color for a printer that is printing, and the red tint on the printing project card. Red is the accent in this wireframe, not a state. Use the semantic status colors for printing, idle and error, and the accent tint for the highlighted card.
6. The placeholder cube icons. Cards show a real project thumbnail area at a fixed aspect ratio, with an empty state for projects that have none.
7. The "5b Work-first" caption and the paragraph below the frame. Annotations, not UI.
8. The empty lower two thirds of the gallery. Show the grid filling the space with enough cards to wrap, so the column count and gutters are visible.

Build with the system, not by hand:
- Components from the Design System page: Button/Primary for New, Button/Secondary for Import and Launch monitor, Chip/Printer, Swatch for filaments, the card and sheet surfaces already there. Create a new component only where none fits, and put it on the Design System page.
- Text: Section for "Projects" and "Printers", Body Bold for names, Body Small for status lines, Label for connection and nozzle, Metadata for the tiniest lines.
- Every gap and padding bound to a Spacing variable; every corner to a Radius variable; every fill and stroke to a Semantic Color variable; every text layer to a text style. No typed numbers, no raw hex.
- The cabinet is 320 wide; the gallery takes the rest. Cards use a 2-column grid at this width with 16 px gutters and grow to 3 columns wider.
- Deliver light and dark. Same layers, different mode.

When done, report: the components you reused and any you created; every value that had no variable or style to bind to, with where it appears; and anything in the wireframe you could not resolve into a design and what you did instead.
```
